# Long reads

::: {.callout-warning}
## First draft
Written from `research/05-long-reads.yml` and not yet reviewed by a second
reader. Three cautions specific to this chapter. Many of its sources are
preprints, because the quantification and benchmarking literature it draws on is
largely unreviewed. Every head-to-head platform comparison in this book's corpus
predates the current nanopore chemistry, so the numbers below describe what was
measured rather than the present state. And @sec-identification names a method
whose authors include the person directing this project, which that section
states where it names it.
:::

A short read reports a fragment, while a long read reports a molecule, and every
result and every failure in this chapter follows from that one difference.

The
practical consequence is joint observation of features that sit far apart in a
transcript. A start site and a poly(A) site, or a splice choice and a chemical
modification, can be seen on the same molecule or seen to be absent from it.
Fragmenting the molecule destroys that pairing, which is why a short-read
protocol cannot substitute for one [@workman2019nanopore]. The same point is
made bluntly by the authors of an isoform-stability method. Isoform-level
stability cannot be estimated from short reads, because the reads cannot be
assigned to isoforms in the first place [@maier2020native].

## SNCA: forty-one isoforms from six exons {#sec-snca}

SNCA is central to Parkinson disease and has six exons. Targeted PacBio
sequencing resolved 41 distinct full-length isoforms from it. The diversity
comes from alternative 5' start sites combined with variable 3' UTR lengths,
on top of the exon-skipping forms already known [@tseng2019landscape].

One of those start sites sits inside intron 4 and had been invisible. It had no
support in GTEx short-read data and no FANTOM5 CAGE peak. A single transcript
in a public direct-RNA dataset confirmed it, and the junction joining it to
exon 5 was separately confirmed by aggregated short-read junction data
[@tseng2019landscape].

A heavily studied disease gene had most of its transcript structures outside
the annotation, and they were reachable by reading whole molecules.

## Distant choices on one molecule can be coupled {#sec-one-molecule}

An entire complex splice chain can be observed rather than inferred. In
Arabidopsis, a single uninterrupted nanopore alignment of 12.7 kb spanning 63
exons matched an annotated isoform exactly, with no junction counting involved
[@parker2020nanopore].

Once whole molecules are available, dependence between distant choices becomes
testable. Each PacBio read of an MCF-7 mRNA reported one complete molecule, so
pairs of processing choices could be tested for statistical dependence within
it. More than 60 per cent of multi-exon genes, 6,825 of 11,350, had at least
one coupled pair of features [@anvar2018fulllength].

Coupling also runs between the two ends of a transcript. Long-read isoform maps
in *Drosophila* identified promoters whose use biases 3' end choice. Deleting
one such promoter from the *orb* locus by CRISPR left the proximal 3' end
expressed while massively depleting the distal one. Those authors conclude that
a dominant promoter can drive read-through of canonical poly(A) signals toward
more distal termination [@alfonsogonzalez2023sites].

Where a transcript starts can determine where it stops, which is a statement
about single molecules and unavailable from fragments.

## One splice chain is not one transcript {#sec-three-axes}

A transcript has three parts that can vary independently: a start site, a
splice chain, and an end site. Annotation has historically collapsed two of
them.

In GENCODE v40 a multi-exon splice chain carries at most three annotated start
or end sites. It is given exactly one start site in 99.7 per cent of cases and
one end site in 99.4 per cent. Long-read annotation attaches substantially more
distinct ends to the same chain [@reese2023encode4].

![One intron chain, with the ends an annotation gives it and the ends observed
on real molecules. The internal structure is identical in every row, which is
what makes them a single splice chain and several distinct
transcripts.](../figures/three-axes.svg){#fig-three-axes width=100%}

Scored on all three parts together, 89.8 per cent of human protein-coding genes
used more than one distinct component across the ENCODE4 long-read samples.
Long non-coding RNAs and pseudogenes were far less variable
[@reese2023encode4].

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## ENCODE4 and GTEx long reads are preprints here

Both the ENCODE4 long-read collection and the GTEx long-read transcriptome
appear in this book's corpus only as preprints, and are cited as such. Every
number taken from either needs re-checking against the peer-reviewed version.
The claim records say so, and the bibliography emits them as preprints rather
than as journal articles.
:::

## The two ends are not equally trustworthy {#sec-ends-evidence}

@sec-three-axes treats a start site, a splice chain and an end site as three
things that vary independently. It does not say how either end is established,
and the two are not established equally well.

The asymmetry is measurable on the same data. Among features in the ENCODE4
human long-read collection that were novel relative to GENCODE, 42.8 per cent of
start sites had CAGE or RAMPAGE support. 79.0 per cent of end sites had
support from PAS-seq or a poly(A) atlas [@reese2023encode4]. A novel 5' end was
about half as likely as a novel 3' end to be corroborated by anything other than
the long reads themselves.

Part of the reason is where reads actually begin. In a reanalysis of published
human long-read data from five cell lines, more than 50 per cent of nanopore
direct-cDNA read starts and more than 40 per cent of direct-RNA read starts fell
outside the gene's first exon [@calvoroitberg2024challenges]. Measured on the
same molecules rather than across datasets, about 80 per cent of nanopore
native-RNA molecules per transcript reached their 3' end while only about 32 per
cent reached the 5' end [@ibrahim2021teraseq].

Selecting for the cap helps and does not solve it. Restricting to molecules
carrying both a cap and a ligated 5' adapter, only about 29 per cent per
transcript reach the annotated 5' end [@ibrahim2021teraseq]. Across ONT
libraries from the same human brain and heart RNA, cap-trapping protocols led on
the share of reads corroborated at both ends, at 43 per cent for one protocol
against 34 per cent for another [@carbonellsala2024captrapseq].

Two bounds keep this from becoming a rule that every short 5' end is an
artefact. The corroborating evidence is itself imperfect and borrowed. The CAGE clusters
used to certify these ends came from samples other than the ones sequenced, so a
read without CAGE support has not been shown to be truncated. Those authors call
their completeness estimates indicative rather than definitive
[@carbonellsala2024captrapseq]. In a head-to-head comparison of six 5'-end sequencing methods on one human RNA
sample, CAGE ranked best for mRNA. It still placed 24 per cent of its reads for
an average gene further from the transcript 5' end than a tenth of the
transcript's length [@adiconis2018comprehensive].

The other bound is biological rather than technical. Cellular stress triggers
decay from the 5' end of
messenger RNAs, and the shortened ends that result leave a signature visible in
short-read data as reduced read density at the 5' end [@dar2023fulllength]. A
molecule that starts downstream of the annotated start may be reporting its own
state accurately.

## Internal priming, and the filter that discards real sites {#sec-internal-priming}

The 3' end has the better evidence and it has a specific failure mode. An
oligo-dT primer cannot tell a poly(A) tail from a run of adenines encoded inside
a transcript, and when it anneals internally the adenines it contributes are
copied into the read. The resulting 3' end is indistinguishable in sequence from
a genuine cleavage and polyadenylation site [@hoque2012analysis].

Because the artefact and the real site look alike in the read, detection has to
use the genome instead. Long-read quality control scores a called 3' end by the
percentage of adenines in a window of genomic sequence immediately downstream of
it [@tardaguila2018sqanti]. In practice that test is a fixed threshold combined
with a reproducibility requirement. One large human and mouse collection kept
only transcripts whose last 20 genomic bases were under 50 per cent adenine, and
separately required five supporting reads across at least two libraries
[@reese2023encode4].

How often it happens depends on the chemistry rather than on the sequence. A mouse 3'-end sequencing study put reads attributable either to internal A-rich
sequence or to short non-templated oligo(A) tails at about 60 per cent of all
reads with a conventional oligo-dT capture. That fell to about 17 per cent with
a 45-thymidine chimeric capture oligo [@hoque2012analysis]. In an Arabidopsis
dataset sequenced without reverse transcription or oligo-dT priming at all, only
27 of 20,972 runs of six or more genomic adenines, 0.13 per cent, had ten or
more read ends just upstream [@sherstnev2012direct].

The filter has a cost that is rarely stated. Genuine poly(A) sites do sit in
A-rich genomic sequence: 5,392 of the mouse sites mapped by a method that avoids
oligo-dT priming, 7.6 per cent of the total, lie in such sequence and would be
discarded by a standard internal-priming filter [@hoque2012analysis]. Those same
authors support them with crosslinking of a cleavage factor around them. The
routine correction is therefore both incomplete and lossy, removing authentic 3'
ends along with artefacts without excluding every artefact
[@sherstnev2012direct].

## Artefacts that pass for isoforms {#sec-artifacts}

A long read can report a structure that was never in the cell.

An intron-within-an-exon event in CD19 turned out to be a reverse transcription
product. On reporter-transfected cells it made up over 25 per cent of PCR-free
direct-cDNA reads and nearly 30 per cent of PCR-amplified cDNA reads, and it
was undetectable in direct RNA reads. Those authors generalise the warning:
any RT-dependent protocol can invent such events [@schulz2021direct].

Spurious 3' ends have a similar explanation. Comparing cDNA and native-RNA
libraries across two species and three platforms, one group argues that the
spurious poly(A) sites usually blamed on internal priming are produced by
template switching instead. Many appeared at sites carrying only three to five
adenines, too few for an oligo-dT primer to bind [@balazs2019template].

An apparent intron can be made by the enzyme rather than by the spliceosome. A
117-nucleotide intron seemingly removed from about 30 per cent of one yeast
non-coding RNA's transcripts was produced by reverse transcription, appearing
with an MMLV-derived enzyme and not with an AMV-derived one
[@houseley2010apparent]. The junction need never have existed in a cell: two
RNAs transcribed separately in vitro, then mixed and reverse transcribed,
reproducibly yielded apparent trans-spliced products [@houseley2010apparent].

Tested experimentally, most reported non-co-linear junctions did not survive. Of
13 previously published human candidates that could be examined, seven were in
vitro artefacts, and some of those had already passed RT-PCR validation
[@yu2014observed]. The same study confirmed others as genuine, so the lesson is
not that non-co-linear junctions are all artefacts.

Removing reverse transcription does not remove the problem. Internal sequencing
adapters, the mark of two molecules joined during library preparation, were found
inside 0.67 to 1.25 per cent of reads in each of five human cell lines from one
public nanopore direct-RNA dataset [@li2026genomic]. Those adapter-bridged joins
were the dominant source of apparent rearrangement rather than a minor one,
accounting for 63 to 85 per cent of all chimeric reads in those samples
[@li2026genomic]. Direct RNA is the right control for an artefact of reverse
transcription, and it is not an artefact-free baseline.

Sequencing error is also not the only explanation for non-canonical novel
junctions. In a PacBio mouse neural transcriptome, template-switching evidence
was enriched in transcripts carrying at least one novel splice site, flagging
7.24 per cent of them against 1.98 per cent of transcripts built only from
annotated splice sites [@tardaguila2018sqanti].

The asymmetry that makes novel structures hard to trust is measurable.
Quality-control analysis of a PacBio mouse neural transcriptome found that 99.9
per cent of junctions already in the annotation used canonical dinucleotides,
against only 69 per cent of the 3,837 novel junctions, leaving 1,188
non-canonical [@tardaguila2018sqanti]. Novel long-read junctions need filtering
before they can be interpreted.

## Platforms, with a date attached {#sec-platforms}

Everything above says a long read reports a molecule. Two instruments do the
reporting, they fail differently, and the numbers that compare them all have a
chemistry and a year attached.

They do not agree on what the molecule was. Sequencing PCR copies of the same
reverse-transcription event on both platforms, a quarter of the paired reads
disagreed on at least one of transcription start site, poly(A) site or a splice
site [@mikheenko2022sequencing]. The errors sit in different places: of those
called against a three-way majority truth, 41 per cent of the PacBio errors and
23 per cent of the nanopore errors fell inside homopolymers
[@mikheenko2022sequencing].

Most of that disagreement about exon structure is slack rather than a different
splice chain. Allowing junctions to differ by up to 6 bp removed 48 per cent of
the disagreements between paired reads. It also reclassified as annotated 43 per
cent of the nanopore mappings and 15 per cent of the PacBio mappings that had
looked annotation-inconsistent at single-base resolution
[@mikheenko2022sequencing]. Where a nanopore splice site lands depends on the
sequence around it as well as on read quality. Annotated donors with a GUGU two
bases downstream were mis-called at that offset in 6.48 per cent of assigned read
introns, against 3.06 per cent at the far commoner GUNNGU donors
[@mikheenko2022sequencing].

Some of the gap belongs to the aligner. With around 10 per cent per-read error
on nanopore R9.4.1 native RNA, spliced alignment recovered 80.7 per cent of mouse
introns as canonical against 98.5 per cent in the reference annotation. Nanopore cDNA from the same samples did worse at 67.7 per cent
[@sessegolo2019transcriptome]. That matters for the canonical-dinucleotide gap
reported in @sec-artifacts, which this chapter had left to sequencing error
alone.

Accuracy can be raised, and each route costs something. Measured in 2018 on one synthetic cDNA pool, median read accuracy ran from 87
per cent for single-pass nanopore to 98.9 per cent for PacBio circular
consensus. In between sat rolling-circle consensus at 94 per cent and
paired-strand nanopore at 95.6 per cent
[@volden2018improving]. Splice-site precision followed it: the share of splice
sites matching an annotated site exactly was 80.4 per cent for single-pass
nanopore, 91.3 per cent after rolling-circle consensus and 96.9 per cent for
PacBio circular consensus [@volden2018improving].

The PacBio route buys accuracy with passes over the same molecule, so insert
length and accuracy trade against each other. The 2019 circular consensus
protocol that produced 99.8 per cent accurate reads averaging 13.5 kb was
designed around needing about ten passes [@wenger2019accurate]. Concatenating
cDNAs trades the other way: its libraries returned 45.3 million reads at the median, where standard Iso-Seq
returned 4.3 million, roughly tenfold. Median mapped read length fell from 2,338 bp to 1,677 bp
[@paniagua2026systematic]. Reading both strands helps only a minority of
molecules, with duplex reads making up 3.33 per cent of one 2022 amplicon run
[@luo2022systematic].

Read length against transcript length is the constraint underneath all of this.
Median mapped read length was 2,338 bp for standard PacBio Iso-Seq, 1,677 bp for
the concatenation protocol and 530 bp for nanopore cDNA on R9.4.1 in one mouse
cohort [@paniagua2026systematic]. In nanopore native-RNA libraries, transcripts
under 2 kb were often covered completely by one read while longer ones rarely
were [@soneson2019comprehensive]. The spike-in sets used to show that long reads
capture whole molecules cannot settle this, because every SIRV and ERCC
transcript is shorter than 2.5 kb while about 17 per cent of Ensembl GRCh38.90
transcripts are longer [@soneson2019comprehensive].

Nanopore accuracy moved a long way between kit generations. On the same cell
line's RNA, median alignment identity was 90.65 per cent for the 2019 kit and
98.67 per cent for the 2024 kit [@ghohabiesfahani2026assessment]. Throughput
moved further: the 2019 dataset took 30 MinION flow cells for 9.4 million aligned
reads. A single PromethION flow cell on the 2024 kit produced 16.6 million
from the same cell line [@ghohabiesfahani2026assessment]. Device, kit and
basecaller all change between those two figures, so it is a generational
comparison rather than a chemistry experiment.

Two results stop that from reading as a clean march forward. The characteristic
nanopore error is a deletion rather than a mismatch, and on the earlier kits
median read accuracy was 87 to 92 per cent with deletions outnumbering both
mismatches and insertions [@liuwei2024sequencing]. The newer kit improved the
error types that matter least here. On synthetic transcripts it read at 93.5 per
cent against 92.1 per cent, and the gain came from fewer mismatches and
insertions while the deletion rate stayed high [@liuwei2024sequencing]. That 93.5
per cent and the 98.67 per cent above are not the same measurement, being
different RNA, different metric and different basecaller, and this book does not
reconcile them.

Raising accuracy also did not improve quantification. In a cell-mixing benchmark
the rolling-circle consensus protocol scored below 0.60 mean Spearman correlation
against expected abundances, while five ordinary cDNA and direct-RNA combinations
reached 0.73 to 0.83 [@pardopalacios2024lrgasp]. Accuracy and depth buy different
things, and the protocols that buy one spend the other.

## Direct RNA sequencing {#sec-direct-rna}

Nanopore can sequence the native RNA strand rather than a cDNA copy of it.
Applied to the GM12878 cell line, that yielded 33,984 isoforms over 10,793
genes, and 52.6 per cent of them carried an exon junction chain absent from
GENCODE [@workman2019nanopore].

The native molecule carries more than its sequence. Reading the poly(A) tail as
part of the same molecule that identified the isoform showed that two isoforms
of DDX5 carry very different tails. The intron-retaining isoform had a median
tail of 327 nucleotides, against 125 for the protein-coding one
[@workman2019nanopore]. Tail length is a per-isoform property, and it had been
measured per gene.

Stability behaves the same way, and metabolic labelling read out on native
nanopore molecules showed that individual isoforms do not share a single
stability response. Under heat shock, the dynamics of individual isoforms varied
globally relative to the combined RNA of their gene [@maier2020native].

Modifications become locatable on identified transcripts, and mapping m6A from
basecalling error on native Arabidopsis RNA connected the modification to a
whole-organism phenotype. The writer mutant had a lengthened circadian period
alongside altered abundance of oscillator transcripts [@parker2020nanopore].

Accuracy was the other half of the problem. An accuracy-boosting
nanopore protocol was applied to a human peripheral blood sample. Its authors
conclude that deep, accurate, full-length cDNA sequencing resolves the hardest
transcripts in the mammalian genome. They offer it as an unbiased replacement
for the dedicated HLA typing and immune-repertoire assays such work normally
requires [@cole2020complete].

Native RNA costs input material as well as throughput. On the 2022 kit in
Escherichia coli it took more than 10 micrograms of starting total RNA to leave
the 500 nanograms of messenger RNA a run requires after ribosomal depletion
[@grunberger2022nanopore]. What it buys, on matched depth-normalised libraries
from one cell line, is transcripts: native-RNA sequencing uniquely detected
12,047 high-confidence transcripts against 2,149 for PCR-cDNA
[@lane2026distinct]. The choice changes the biological answer and not only the
read statistics, since on the same stimulated cells the two protocols shared
only 173 differentially expressed genes out of 218 called from PCR-cDNA and 899
from direct RNA [@lane2026distinct].

Selecting on the poly(A) tail decides what can appear at all. A
non-polyadenylated synthetic transcript spiked into total RNA before oligo-dT
purification was not detected by the subsequent nanopore sequencing, and about
98 per cent of molecules in those libraries carried tails
[@ibrahim2021teraseq]. Depleting ribosomal RNA instead changes which transcripts
exist in the data: in blood libraries only the ribosomal-depleted ones detected
any transcript longer than 50 kb [@natrajgayathri2026polya].

Annotation is still catching up, including in genomes that have been available
for a long time. The Arabidopsis authors note that a genome sequence available
since 2000 still had annotation left to fix [@parker2020nanopore]. In maize,
long reads corrected gene models rather than merely adding to them. RGH3 had
been mis-annotated because of a genome assembly error, and CSR1 was present in
the reference sequence with no annotation at all [@wang2016unveiling].

## Identifying isoforms from RNA-seq {#sec-identification}

Everything so far concerns what the reads are. This section concerns what is done
with them, because an isoform is not read off a dataset but decided by a
procedure. The approaches below differ in what they assume, and those assumptions
are where the answers diverge.

### Short reads: a graph and a parsimony rule

Reference-guided short-read assembly turns reconstruction into a graph problem
with an explicitly parsimonious objective. Fragment alignments become nodes, an
edge joins two overlapping fragments whose implied introns agree exactly, and the
isoform set reported is the smallest collection of paths covering every fragment
[@trapnell2010transcript]. The general form is a per-locus splice graph. Its vertices are whole or partial
exons and its edges are the junctions seen in spliced alignments, with coverage
as weights. A candidate isoform is a path through it, so reconstruction is the
choice of a path set [@shao2017scallop].

Minimising the number of transcripts does not pick a single answer. Several
smallest path covers can explain the same fragments, so the approach needs a
second criterion, and uneven coverage along the locus supplies it. Per-fragment
inclusion ratios weight the choice among equally parsimonious assemblies
[@trapnell2010transcript]. That tie-break is the practical face of the formal
result in @sec-short-read-limit. Where the likelihood has a flat optimum, the
answer reported is whichever one the secondary criterion prefers.

Parsimony need not be applied everywhere in a splice graph. At least one design applies it only
where the reads leave a branch point undetermined, following the reads where they
span enough exons to constrain how a vertex decomposes, and minimising the
mismatch between inferred and observed coverage otherwise [@shao2017scallop].
The assumption is doing visible work, and it can be narrowed.

### Without a reference genome

Assembly without a genome replaces the splice graph with a de Bruijn graph over
short overlapping subsequences of the reads, in which a candidate transcript is
any path [@grabherr2011trinity]. The method assumes no genome, no gene boundary
and no known splice site, and inherits instead a graph whose enumerable paths are
mostly not transcripts.

Its ceiling is set by the library rather than by the algorithm. A k-mer graph can
only reconstruct a transcript whose whole sequence is covered by adjacent
overlapping k-mers present in the read set, so the recoverable set is fixed
before any assembler runs [@grabherr2011trinity]. What it achieves on
near-identical sequences depends on expression rather than on similarity alone.
Across 77 fission yeast gene families holding 185 paralogues, every member was
recovered at full length for 33 families and some members for another 33. All 26 genes of the remaining 11 families were missed, the misses often being
lowly expressed [@grabherr2011trinity].

### Long reads: collapsing, correcting, clustering

The obvious long-read procedure is to collapse reads sharing an intron chain and
call each group an isoform. It under-reports, because the premise that a long
read is a whole molecule often fails. Whether a sequenced cDNA carries all the
splice sites of its template depends on how completely reverse transcription ran,
which is why assembling long reads recovers structures that collapsing them does
not [@tung2019quantifying].

Collapsing also needs a tolerance, since exact agreement is unattainable at
long-read error rates. One rule merges predicted transcripts carrying the same
number of splice positions when each position agrees to within ten base pairs,
trading structural resolution for precision [@tung2019quantifying]. A consensus
across reads is required rather than optional. Alignments of reads from one locus
routinely disagree about where the splice sites are, and about whether short
exons are present at all [@kovaka2019stringtie2].

Error-tolerant clustering decides which differences between reads are real. One
method corrects reads only half of the way to their cluster's consensus, then
re-partitions and repeats until no cluster holds internal differences, so the
surviving distinct sequences become the candidates [@sahlin2018isocon]. Whether
two near-identical candidates are separate isoforms is then a statistical
question rather than a threshold. The reads assigned to each are tested at the
positions where the candidates differ, for whether sequencing error explains the
evidence better. A candidate keeps the least significant result from all its
pairwise tests [@sahlin2018isocon].

Correcting against the annotation carries an annotation-shaped bias. In one
pipeline a non-canonical junction survives into the output only if the reference
annotation already contains it. So a genuinely novel non-canonical junction is
removed by the same rule that removes a sequencing error
[@wyman2019technology]. Discovery can also hold novelty and familiarity to
different standards by design. In that pipeline a structure already in the
annotation is accepted on sight. An unannotated structure must be seen by
at least five reads in each of at least two biological replicates
[@wyman2019technology]. @sec-quantification returns to what such thresholds cost.

How much of an answer belongs to the annotation is measurable, and the
dependence is steep. With only a fifth of one chromosome's annotation supplied, a
method that identifies isoforms by reporting annotated transcripts covered by
reads fell to 30 per cent sensitivity and 50 per cent precision. Assembling
the same reads gave 74 and 80 per cent [@kovaka2019stringtie2].

One framework makes the ambiguity of partial reads explicit before any isoform is
proposed. Each strand-specific alignment to the reference genome is decomposed into its
path through a splice graph. That graph's nodes include exon segments, junctions
and inferred start and end sites. Reads structurally indistinguishable on it are
grouped into compatibility classes, and candidate isoforms are built by merging
compatible classes [@yu2026lraa]. The same framework runs in
three regimes differing only in how much of the annotation is trusted, from
assigning reads to a supplied annotation without discovery, through using known
structures to guide discovery, to discovery from alignments and genome sequence
alone [@yu2026lraa]. Annotation dependence is a settable input there rather than
a fixed property of the method.

::: {.callout-important}
## A disclosure

That last method is LRAA, and the preprint describing it lists the person
directing this book as an author and gives his address as one of two
corresponding addresses for the work [@yu2026lraa]. It is named here because he
asked for it to be included among the long-read methods. The two records behind
the description above are its authors' own account of what the approach does, no
claim that it outperforms anything is made or cited, and the preprint's own
comparative claim was deliberately not used.
:::

### Short reads against long reads, measured

On the same RNA from the same four donors, short-read and long-read
reconstruction agreed about most novel splicing inside known genes. Of 2,999
such transcripts found in total, 2,377, or 79.2 per cent, were seen by both
platforms in at least one sample [@iwabuchi2026systematic]. The disagreement was
lopsided: 464 novel spliced transcripts came only from short reads against 158
only from long reads. Those authors offer inference-driven short-read false
positives or insufficient long-read coverage without choosing between them
[@iwabuchi2026systematic].

That comparison carries a confound worth stating with it. The long-read libraries
returned about 7.6 million reads in total, against an average of 138.2 million
per sample across four short-read libraries [@iwabuchi2026systematic]. Any count
favouring short reads there has a depth explanation available.

Comparing whole intron chains rather than single junctions shows how partly each
captures the other. With a twenty-base tolerance a short-read assembly held 64.6
per cent of the PacBio chains from the same sample. A nanopore sample and
its short-read assembly held 83.5 and 72.3 per cent of each other
[@wilks2020longtron]. The tolerance is necessary because imprecision in one
junction coordinate does not stay local. It compounds along the chain, so an
exactly matching whole structure becomes less likely the more junctions it has
[@wilks2020longtron].

Where no reference genome exists the two split on completeness rather than on
count. From the same sugarcane experiment, long-read isoform sequencing yielded
39,999 full-length isoforms against 33,762 from short-read de novo assembly. 93.5 per cent of its transcripts carried an open reading frame against 54.2 per
cent of the assembled contigs [@hoang2017survey]. The two datasets were not
matched, so the comparison bounds nothing tightly.

One result should discourage the obvious remedy. Sequencing more deeply does not
make long-read identification more precise. For methods that do not correct
read errors before deciding structures it makes precision worse, because extra
depth supplies extra error-bearing reads from which extra false structures can be
built [@su2024assessment].

### A tension this book has to own

Every long-read method above identifies an isoform by its splice chain, with a
coordinate tolerance. @sec-three-axes argues that a transcript has three
independent parts and that collapsing a splice chain onto one transcript is
exactly what an annotation should not do. The methods the field actually uses
make that collapse, and then recover the ends separately or not at all. The
argument of this chapter and the practice of its tools are not aligned, and
@sec-ends-evidence is the reason the practice persists.

## Quantification apportions rather than counts {#sec-quantification}

Identifying isoforms produces a list of structures. Attaching numbers to them is a separate
procedure, and the number a quantifier reports is not a count.

Before any abundance is estimated, the data for one gene are reduced to a
read-by-isoform compatibility matrix, with an entry of one where that read could
have come from that isoform. The unknowns are one relative abundance per isoform,
constrained to sum to one across the gene [@hu2021liqa]. The iteration that
solves for them starts from the assumption that every isoform is equally
expressed, and stops when the log likelihood stops rising appreciably
[@hu2021liqa]. What is reported is the fixed point of alternating between
apportioning ambiguous reads and re-estimating abundances.

Ambiguous reads are not a corner case. Between 13.8 and 49.5 per cent of reads
matched more than one transcript across the nanopore samples examined in one
study, and those reads are apportioned rather than discarded
[@chen2023context]. Truncation is the reason that ambiguity is common. In a deeply sequenced nanopore cDNA
dataset only 25.7 per cent of reads covered at least 95 per cent of the bases of
the transcript they were assigned to. The mean coverage of a transcript by
one read was 50.4 per cent [@dong2022benchmarking].

The incomplete-match case of @sec-transcript-classes is explicit in the
bookkeeping. Reads are pooled into classes by their compatible transcript set,
and one class holds reads whose junction chain matches one transcript exactly
while also being a subset of longer ones [@chen2023context]. That is precisely
where a genuinely short isoform and a truncated copy of a long one cannot be
told apart.

Long reads also lose a term that short-read methods rely on. Short-read
quantification draws much of its power to separate similar isoforms from a
transcript-length term. So long-read methods that simply delete that term lose
discriminating power with it; one replacement favours assignments that make
coverage along a transcript more uniform [@zarejousheghani2025oarfish].

Two incompatible conventions exist for an ambiguous read. Several quantifiers
apply no mapping-quality filter and let the apportioning spread each read's
weight over all its candidates. One widely used pipeline instead adopted a
minimum mapping quality of one, which in its own spike-in benchmark excluded
5,469 of 21,456 reads [@parthiban2026transcript]. A quality filter is also an
abundance filter: on spike-ins with known input proportions, raising the minimum
progressively over-represented single-isoform genes and under-represented genes
with four annotated isoforms [@parthiban2026transcript]. That is the direction
that makes a complex locus look quieter than it is.

### Read-support thresholds and what they cost

Thresholds exist because probabilistic assignment will give expression to
something that has none. Artificial exon-skipping isoforms inserted into an
annotation received non-zero estimates, and raising a counts-per-million
threshold reduced how many of them appeared [@chen2023context].

They usually act before a catalogue exists rather than on one. One joint-calling
method discards by default any group of identically spliced reads with fewer
than three reads of support summed across the whole cohort. So a structure seen
once or twice never reaches the stage where it could be quantified
[@dolzhenko2026isocall]. Raising the bar mostly deletes novel isoforms rather
than annotated ones, because the novel calls are the lowly expressed ones
[@jetzinger2025join].

One threshold behaves backwards when samples are combined. A minimum-fraction
filter requires a transcript to hold some minimum share of its gene's
expression. So pooling reads across samples raises the gene total and can push
below the threshold a transcript that passed in every sample analysed separately
[@jetzinger2025join].

### Does non-identifiability survive longer reads

@sec-short-read-limit records that different sets of transcript abundances can
generate the same short-read data with equal likelihood. The honest answer for
long reads has three layers that point different ways, and the book states them
separately rather than averaging them.

Per-read ambiguity partly survives the move to long reads. In the one head-to-head test of class size,
the mean number of transcripts in the equivalence class a read fell into was
almost identical for nanopore and for Illumina reads, on the same annotation and
index [@soneson2019comprehensive]. Part of that belongs to the annotation rather
than to the reads. When error-free full-length transcript sequences were used as
idealised reads, 87 per cent fell into classes holding a single transcript,
leaving about an eighth compatible with more than one annotated isoform even in
that ideal case [@soneson2019comprehensive].

Measured uncertainty mostly collapses once reads are longer. By a variance-based measure of assignment
ambiguity on matched libraries from the same cell lines, every transcript in the
nanopore data had an over-dispersion coefficient between 1 and 1.15, while
two-thirds of transcripts in the Illumina data exceeded 3.56
[@dong2022benchmarking]. Those two results use different measures, different
mappers and chemistries three years apart, which is why they are reported side by
side.

The formal version makes read length the variable. Non-identifiability can be
stated as a rank condition. For a worked four-transcript gene with 200 base-pair
exons, the matrix relating isoform abundances to expected read counts stays
rank-deficient at every read length below 600 base pairs. The
maximum-likelihood solution is then a line of equally good answers rather than a
point [@zhang2026quantifying]. Lengthening reads relieves that for most genes
and not for all, with the condition number falling monotonically for most and
rising transiently for a minority [@zhang2026quantifying].

Residual error is measurable on a named gene. FAM219A had a mean absolute
relative difference of 0.7094 when quantified from 150 base-pair paired short
reads and 0.5858 from long reads alone. So the long-read estimate improved and
remained wrong by more than half [@li2025improving]. Long reads improved the estimate for that gene without bringing its error near
zero [@li2025improving].

So the problem is weakened sharply in practice and not dissolved in principle.
The formal result is derived for reads of one fixed length. Nothing in this
book's corpus re-derives it for reads that are long but truncated from one end,
which is the actual long-read case.

Two benchmarks keep the practical claim modest. Against spike-ins with known
abundances, a short-read quantifier recovered the truth better than any long-read
method entered, with an average Spearman correlation of 0.84 against 0.29 to
0.78 [@pardopalacios2024lrgasp]. And across three long-read protocols run on the
same eight cell lines, the protocols picked the same major isoform for only 67 to
69 per cent of multi-isoform genes [@you2025longbench].

## Phasing comes free with read length {#sec-phasing}

A read long enough to span a heterozygous site carries its own phase
information. In a polymorphic mouse cross, one heterozygous site inside a read
was enough to assign that whole transcript to a parental chromosome
[@lemoine2025longread]. Phasing is cheap in information terms, and it comes
free with length.

Assigning native RNA reads to a parental chromosome this way gave allelic
imbalance for 228 of the testable autosomal genes, which is 6.1 per cent. Among
X-linked genes 23 showed imbalance, 22 of them maternal, and the single
paternal one was XIST [@workman2019nanopore].

The same approach measures escape from X inactivation in transcripts rather than
in junction counts. In a mouse model with skewed inactivation, only 69 of 12,623
X-linked long reads came from the inactive chromosome, which is 0.54 per cent.
Xist plus the two known escape genes accounted for 39 of those few
[@lemoine2025longread].

## Single-cell long reads {#sec-sc-longread}

The barrier to single-cell isoform work was arithmetic, and its authors set it
out. The work needs reads beyond about 5 kb at depths above twenty million, and
no platform delivered both. Ligating cDNAs into composite molecules raised
PacBio output more than fifteenfold, to roughly 40 million reads per run
[@alkhafaji2024highthroughput].

@sec-brain-atlas takes up what that throughput bought. It fixes throughput and
leaves cost where it was, though. Authors applying the same approach to
Alzheimer brain state the ceiling directly. Even with the gain from
concatenation, depth per sequencing run remains lower and cost per read higher
than for short-read sequencing [@shahnaee2026rna].

## Full-length chemistry reaches more splicing {#sec-sc-chemistry}

What the extra length buys in a single cell has been measured on one sample. In
the same human individual, droplet data yielded computable splicing scores for
1,416 genes against 9,802 for plate-based full-length data. Those authors
state that 3'-biased droplet reads never reach some splicing events at all
[@olivieri2021splicing]. Because the alternatively spliced exons of PTPRC sit
near the 5' end of the transcript, 3' gene-expression libraries left under a
tenth of cells positive for either CD45 isoform even at saturating depth
[@michalik2024ideis].

The bias is less simple than it sounds. In one 3'-biased chemistry, junction
recovery did not fall off toward the 5' end of genes. Recall was slightly lower
close to the 3' terminus than tens of kilobases upstream, which complicates the
assumption that 3' counting is uniformly blind to upstream splicing
[@saferali2026framework].

What has been found with that reach sits later in the book. @sec-isoform-only
has the share of isoform variation that gene-level counting cannot explain,
@sec-brain-atlas charges regional differences to one compartment, and
@sec-sc-methods separates two T cell states by one receptor's isoform.

## Long reads cost depth in cells, junctions in bulk {#sec-longread-cost}

The two costs below were measured in different settings and should not be
pooled. The depth penalty comes from a single-cell comparison; the junction
penalty comes from bulk libraries.

Isoform resolution is bought with sequencing depth. In a matched single-cell
comparison on the same cells, PacBio concatenation
libraries averaged roughly 21,000 to 97,000 reads per cell against roughly
142,000 to 443,000 for the Illumina libraries [@zajac2025comparison].

Filtering at the analysis stage removes more again. The standard single-cell
long-read pipeline in that comparison discarded an average of 48 per cent of
isoforms and 27 per cent of reads as low-coverage or non-canonical, with the
loss biased toward longer transcripts [@zajac2025comparison]. Filtering novel
structures is necessary, and it is not free.

Junction sensitivity is the clearest remaining deficit in bulk. On matched
libraries, short-read splicing analysis still recovered about 30 per cent more
splice junctions than either long-read platform [@han2024contrasting], so long
reads add structure at a cost in junction sensitivity. That comparison ran on
bulk data only. It used human cell line replicates from LRGASP, heart, brain and
liver samples from GTEx. One patient-derived leukaemia line, subsampled so
that total bases sequenced were comparable across platforms, and no single-cell
data entered it at all [@han2024contrasting].

The proposed explanation is that molecules are not captured end to end. In the
LRGASP data only 5.4 per cent of ONT reads and 51.6 per cent of PacBio reads
reached the roughly 3 kb median human transcript length. Events far from the
poly(A) end were correspondingly harder to quantify [@han2024contrasting]. A
long read is often not long enough to reach them.

The same comparison runs the other way for one event class. Long reads detected
far more unique intron-retention events, about 10,000 for PacBio and 6,300 for
Nanopore against roughly 2,400 from the short-read analysis, which those authors
read as the two technologies being complementary [@han2024contrasting]. What
long reads buy in single cells is the subject of @sec-isoform-only and
@sec-brain-atlas.

## Variants read against full-length transcripts {#sec-gtex-lr}

Transcript structure changes what a variant is predicted to do. Adding
long-read transcripts to the reference annotation changed the predicted most
severe consequence for 0.67 per cent of GTEx genome variants. The
reassigned variants carried higher average CADD scores than those whose
annotation was unchanged [@glinos2021transcriptome].

Haplotype resolution collapses ambiguous associations into single statements.
In GTEx tissues, haplotype-resolved long reads reduced a cluster of overlapping
splicing associations at DUSP13 to one. In both donors showing allelic
transcript-structure imbalance, the transcript missing four internal exons was
the more highly expressed from the risk allele of a body-fat-associated locus
[@glinos2021transcriptome].

The same logic names candidate effectors at scale. Pairing colocalised splicing
QTLs with long-read transcripts from a bone-relevant cell model nominated 2,029
full-length protein isoforms, 643 of them unannotated, across 441 genes, as
candidate effectors of bone mineral density associations [@abood2024longread].

Nanopore sequencing of B cells from 67 donors mapped 17,119 isoform-level
expression QTLs touching 5,502 isoforms of 3,958 genes, against only 6,350
gene-level eQTLs in the same data [@nagura2025longread]. Of those isoform-level
associations, 70.6 per cent were not detected by a gene-level analysis of the
same data [@nagura2025longread].

A gene-level scan of that cohort would have reported a result, and would have
missed most of what was there.
